context_blurb:
Kick a ball, and your body works as a team. Bones hold you up, and muscles pull on them. Two messenger systems give the orders: nerves flash electrical signals in an instant, while glands send slower chemical messages, called hormones, through the blood.

A newborn has close to three hundred bones, a grown-up only 206. Many start as separate pieces joined by cartilage, a firm, rubbery tissue. As the child grows, the cartilage hardens into bone and the pieces fuse into single bones, so none is lost.

Red marrow, a soft tissue inside bones, makes the blood cells. A baby's marrow is nearly all red, but much turns yellow with growth. In a grown-up, the hollow shaft of the thigh bone holds yellow marrow, made mostly of fat, which makes no blood cells. Adult blood comes from red marrow in the hips, ribs, breastbone, skull and backbone.

A muscle moves a bone by contracting, or shortening, to pull it; it can never push. So muscles work in pairs, one shortening while its partner relaxes. The quadriceps, down the front of your thigh, straightens the knee, and the hamstrings behind bend it. In a kick, the backswing is the hamstrings' work, and then the quadriceps shortens and the hamstrings relax. Straighten your leg with a hand on your thigh, and feel the quadriceps firm up.

Hair and nails grow from living roots in the skin, but the parts you see are dead cells packed with keratin, a tough protein, so trimming them does not hurt. A hair's root, though, is wrapped in nerve endings, so pulling one out stings.

In the eye, the clear cornea and the lens behind it bend light into a sharp, upside-down picture at the back of the eye. There, in the retina, light-sensing cells called rods and cones turn the picture into electrical signals, which the optic nerve carries to the brain. The coloured iris only sets the size of the pupil.

Step on a tack, and your foot jerks up in a reflex, a movement made without thinking. A sensory nerve, which carries news from the senses, takes the signal to the spinal cord, and a motor nerve, which carries orders, takes the cord's reply straight back to the leg muscles. The signal reaches the brain too, so the sting is felt a moment after the foot has moved.

Because the spinal cord carries signals both ways, news up to the brain and orders down to the muscles, a cut clean through it takes away feeling and movement below the injury. A patient hurt mid-back cannot feel or move the legs, though the legs are unhurt.

Glands release hormones into the blood, which carries them all over the body. The pituitary, a pea-sized gland under the brain, makes growth hormone and is called the master gland, since its hormones set other glands working. Robert Wadlow had an overgrown pituitary; at his death in 1940, aged 22, he stood 2.72 metres, the tallest person ever recorded. The extra hormone reached his leg bones by travelling in his blood, for nerves carry electrical signals, not hormones.

The thyroid, a butterfly-shaped gland in the neck, sets how fast cells burn the fuel from food. When it makes far too much hormone, cells burn food faster than it comes in, so a woman with the problem loses weight though she eats more, and she feels hot, with a racing heart.

Insulin, made by the pancreas, lets the body's cells take sugar in from the blood to use or store, so the blood's sugar level falls. In diabetes, too much sugar stays in the blood. In January 1922 Leonard Thompson, a boy of 13 or 14 dying of diabetes in Toronto, got the first insulin injection, made from animal pancreases by Frederick Banting and Charles Best. It caused an allergic reaction, but twelve days later James Collip's purer extract dropped his blood sugar from 520 to 120 within about a day, and he lived about thirteen more years.

A nerve signal acts within thousandths of a second and stops with the signalling, but a hormone works as long as it stays in the blood. In a fright, the adrenal glands, on top of the kidneys, pour out adrenaline, which speeds the heart and sends extra sugar into the blood. A girl startled by a firework jumps at once, but her heart pounds on for minutes, because the adrenaline keeps acting until her body clears it.
